title: Theorem A
body_md:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain and let $K=\operatorname{Frac} R$.
The following conditions are equivalent: $R$ is Gorenstein Pr\"ufer;
every overring $R\subseteq T\subseteq K$ is Gorenstein flat as an
$R$-module; and every finitely generated $R$-subalgebra of $K$ is
Gorenstein flat as an $R$-module.
head: environment

label: def:overring-homological
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:overring-homological}
A module $M$ is \emph{Gorenstein flat} if it is a cycle of an exact
complex of flat modules that remains exact after tensoring with every
injective module. The class of such modules is denoted by $\mathcal{GF}(R)$.
Its associated dimension $\operatorname{Gfd}_R M$ is the least length of a finite
resolution by Gorenstein flat modules, and is infinity when no such
resolution exists. We put $\operatorname{Gfd}_R0=0$.
An $R$-module $M$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$, or is
\emph{super finitely presented}, if it admits an exact sequence
\[
 \cdots\longrightarrow F_2\longrightarrow F_1
 \longrightarrow F_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0,
\]
where each $F_i$ is a finitely generated free $R$-module.
Equivalently, one may require each $F_i$ to be finitely generated
projective. We denote the class of these modules by
$\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$. A module is \emph{totally reflexive}
if it is a cycle of an exact complex of finitely generated free modules
whose $R$-dual is exact. A domain is \emph{Gorenstein Pr\"ufer} if it is
coherent and $\operatorname{wGgldim}(R):=\sup_M\operatorname{Gfd}_RM\le1$.
head: environment

label: lem:finite-factorization
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{(i) Factoring through a finite free module.}\enspace Take a presentation $R^r\to N$ with kernel $L$, and choose
$\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_s\in L$ spanning $K\otimes_R L$. Express the flat
target as a filtered colimit of finitely generated free modules by
Lazard's theorem \cite[Tag~058G]{Stacks}. The map from $R^r$ factors at
some stage, and a later stage kills all the $\ell_i$. For every
$\ell\in L$ there is $0\ne d\in R$ with
$d\ell\in\sum_iR\ell_i$. Torsion-freeness of that free stage then kills
$\ell$, so the factorization descends to $N$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{(ii) Extending maps into a flat module.}\enspace Write $F^+=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(F,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$.
Since $F^+$ is injective, character duality gives
\[
 \operatorname{Ext}_R^1(N,F^{++})\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(F^+,N)^+=0.
\]
Let $h:L\to F$ be a map on the kernel of a presentation by a finitely generated free module
$R^r\to N$. Extend $h$ to $R^r\to F^{++}$. Choose finitely many
relations spanning $K\otimes_RL$ as in (i). The corresponding finite
system of linear equations, whose constants are their images under
$h$, has a solution in $F^{++}$. Purity of $F\to F^{++}$ gives a
solution in $F$. The resulting map $R^r\to F$ agrees with $h$ on
these relations. Clearing denominators and using torsion-freeness of
$F$ proves agreement on all of $L$. Hence $\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(N,F)=0$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-finite-dual
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-finite-dual}
Let $R$ be a domain and $M$ a finitely generated Gorenstein flat $R$-module.
Then the evaluation map $M\to M^{**}$ is an isomorphism,
$M^*\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$, and
$\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(M^*,R)=0$ for $i>0$.  Also $\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(M,F)=0$ for every flat
$R$-module $F$.  If in addition $M\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$, then $M$ and
$M^*$ are totally reflexive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: a finite free coresolution.}\enspace Choose $0\to M\to F_0\to G\to0$ with $F_0$ flat and $G$ Gorenstein flat.
Factor the first map through a finitely generated free module $P$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-factorization}(i).
The resulting map $M\to P$ is injective.  For every injective $E$, the map
$E\otimes_R M\to E\otimes_R P$ is injective, since its composite into
$E\otimes_R F_0$ is injective.  Hence the cokernel $M_1=P/M$ satisfies
$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(E,M_1)=0$.  The cokernel criterion
\cite[Theorem~2.3]{BennisGF} makes $M_1$ Gorenstein flat.  Iterating gives
\[
 0\longrightarrow M_j\longrightarrow P_j\longrightarrow M_{j+1}
 \longrightarrow0\quad(j\ge0),\qquad M_0=M,
\]
with all $P_j$ finitely generated free and all $M_j$ finitely generated
Gorenstein flat.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: finite duals and reflexivity.}\enspace By Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-factorization}(ii), dualizing the displayed
short exact sequences gives
\[
 0\longrightarrow M_{j+1}^*\longrightarrow P_j^*
 \longrightarrow M_j^*\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular every $M_j^*$ is finitely generated, and splicing gives a
resolution by finitely generated free modules of $M^*$.  Dualizing $P_j^*\to M_j^*$
embeds $M_j^{**}$ into $P_j$.  It contains $M_j$ under the evaluation map.
For a finitely generated torsion-free module, clearing denominators in a
fraction-field dual basis shows that evaluation becomes an isomorphism
over $K$.  Here $M_j^*$ is finitely generated as well, so
$M_j^{**}/M_j$ is torsion.  It embeds in the torsion-free module
$P_j/M_j=M_{j+1}$, and is therefore zero.  The dual of the spliced
resolution of $M^*$ is thus the original exact coresolution.  It gives
$\operatorname{Ext}_R^{>0}(M^*,R)=0$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: total reflexivity in type $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$.}\enspace If $M\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$, every syzygy in a resolution by finitely generated free modules is finitely generated and Gorenstein flat.  The degree-one
vanishing already proved gives $\operatorname{Ext}_R^{>0}(M,R)=0$.  Splicing this
resolution with the dual of a resolution by finitely generated free modules of $M^*$ gives
a totally acyclic complex of finitely generated free modules.  Its dual treats $M^*$ as well.
For an injective $E$, tensoring such a complex is the same as applying
$\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,E)$ to its exact dual.  Thus the complexes are also complete
flat resolutions.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-rank-one
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-rank-one}
Let $R$ be a domain with quotient field $K$. If $G\subseteq K$ is a
Gorenstein flat $R$-module and $0\ne N\subseteq G$ is a finitely
generated fractional submodule, then $N_v\subseteq G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Embed $G$ into a flat module $F$ with Gorenstein flat, hence torsion-free,
cokernel.  Factor $N\to F$ through a finitely generated free module by
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-factorization}(i).  Each coordinate map $N\to R$ is multiplication by an element of
$(R:N)$.  For $x\in N_v$ all these coordinate values lie in $R$, so $x$
belongs to $F$, with the identification on the line $KG\subseteq KF$.
Some $0\ne d\in R$ satisfies $dx\in N$.  Torsion-freeness of $F/G$ then
puts $x$ in $G$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-normal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $0\ne a,b\in R$, put $x=b/a$, $S=R[x]$, $T=R[x^{-1}]$, and
$U=R[x,x^{-1}]$.  Integral closedness gives $S\cap T=R$, whereas
$S+T=U$; see \cite[Tag~052J]{Stacks}.  Thus
\[
 0\longrightarrow R\longrightarrow S\oplus T\longrightarrow U
 \longrightarrow0
\]
is exact.  Choose an injective cogenerator $E$ of $R$-modules; thus
$\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,E)\ne0$ for every nonzero $N$. Since $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(E,U)=0$, the map
$E\to(E\otimes_R S)\oplus(E\otimes_R T)$ is injective.

Let $I=(a,b)R$. The trace ideal of $I$ is $II^{-1}$.
If $II^{-1}\ne R$, choose $0\ne e\in E$ killed by
$II^{-1}$.  Every relation $ra+sb=0$ is $(r,s)=(bc,-ac)$ for
$c\in I^{-1}$.  Consequently the prescriptions
$(a,b)\mapsto(e,0)$ and $(a,b)\mapsto(0,e)$ define maps $I\to E$.
Extending them to $R$ gives $e_1,e_2\in E$ with
$ae_1=e$, $be_1=0$, $ae_2=0$, $be_2=e$.
Then $e\otimes1=be_2\otimes1=ae_2\otimes x=0$ in $E\otimes_R S$,
and similarly it is zero in $E\otimes_R T$.  This contradicts the
injection.  Hence every nonzero two-generated ideal is invertible,
which is the classical Pr\"ufer criterion.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-divisorial-maximal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-divisorial-maximal}
Let $(D,\mathfrak n,k)$ be a local domain satisfying $\mathrm{(O)}$.  If its nonzero
maximal ideal is divisorial and not principal, then
$U=(D:\mathfrak n)$ is a proper overring, $U=D+Dx$ for some $x$, and
$(D:U)=\mathfrak n$.  In particular, $U$ is module-finite and
$\dim_k(U/\mathfrak n)=2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: the inverse ring and algebraicity.}\enspace The ideal $\mathfrak n(D:\mathfrak n)$ equals either $\mathfrak n$ or
$D$.  The latter would make $\mathfrak n$ invertible, hence principal.
Thus $U=(\mathfrak n:\mathfrak n)$ is a ring.  Divisoriality gives
$(D:U)=\mathfrak n$ and $U\ne D$.

For $x\in U\setminus D$, maximality gives
$(D:D+Dx)=\mathfrak n$, whence $(D+Dx)_v=U$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-rank-one} applied to the Gorenstein flat overring
$D[x]$ yields $U=D[x]$.  Write $\alpha=x+\mathfrak n$.  If $\alpha$
were transcendental over $k$, then $x^2\notin D$, and the same reasoning
would give $U=D[x^2]$, contradicting $k[\alpha]\ne k[\alpha^2]$.
Thus $\alpha$ is algebraic.  Lifting a monic relation to $f(X)\in D[X]$
gives $f(x)\in\mathfrak n\subset D$; the polynomial $f(X)-f(x)$ shows
that $x$ is integral.  Hence $U$ is module-finite.  Its conductor is
finitely generated by Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-finite-dual}.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: the residue dimension.}\enspace Put $d=\dim_k(U/\mathfrak n)\ge2$, and lift a basis beginning with $1$
to $1,t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}\in U$.  Since $\mathfrak nU=\mathfrak n\subset D$,
these elements generate $U$ over $D$, and comparison modulo
$\mathfrak n$ gives an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathfrak n^{\oplus(d-1)}\longrightarrow D^d
 \longrightarrow U\longrightarrow0.
\]
As $\operatorname{Ext}_D^1(U,D)=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_D(\mathfrak n,D)=U$, duality gives
$D^d\twoheadrightarrow U^{\oplus(d-1)}$.  Reduction modulo
$\mathfrak n$ yields $d(d-1)\le d$, so $d=2$.  A lift of the second
basis element now gives $U=D+Dx$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-seminormal-conductor
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Seminormality means that $z^2,z^3\in D$, $z\in\operatorname{Frac} D$, imply $z\in D$.
It also implies that if all sufficiently large powers of $z$ belong to
$D$, then $z\in D$.  Indeed, the least such threshold $n>1$ would put
both $(z^{n-1})^2$ and $(z^{n-1})^3$ in $D$, lowering the threshold.
For $B=(D:U)$, let $z\in U$ satisfy $z^n\in B$.  For every $u\in U$ and
$j\ge n$, $(zu)^j=z^n z^{j-n}u^j\in B\subseteq D$.  Thus $zu\in D$ for
all $u$, which means $z\in B$.
head: environment

label: thm:qcs-quadratic-witness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:qcs-quadratic-witness}
Let $R$ be a domain satisfying $\mathrm{(O)}$, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec} R$.
If $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is not integrally closed, there is $z\in\operatorname{Frac} R$
such that
\[
 z\notin R_{\mathfrak p},\qquad z^2=u+vz\quad(u,v\in R).
\]
In particular $T=R+Rz$ is a proper module-finite overring, its conductor
$C=(R:T)$ is nonzero and finitely generated, and $C\subseteq\mathfrak p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: a local quadratic witness.}\enspace Work over the local domain $D=R_{\mathfrak p}$, which satisfies
$\mathrm{(O)}$.  If $D$ is not seminormal, choose $y\notin D$ with
$y^2,y^3\in D$.  Then $D+Dy$ is already a quadratic module overring.

Suppose instead that $D$ is seminormal but not normal.  Choose an
integral $y\notin D$ and put $U=D[y]$.  The conductor $B=(D:U)$ is nonzero
and finitely generated by Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-finite-dual}; it is radical
by Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-seminormal-conductor}.  Let $\mathfrak q$ be a
minimal prime over $B$ and set $D'=D_{\mathfrak q}$, $U'=U_{\mathfrak q}$.
Because $U$ is module-finite, conductors commute with this localization.
Hence
\[
 (D':U')=B_{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak qD'=\mathfrak n.
\]
This is a nonzero proper ideal, so $U'\ne D'$.  It is divisorial, being
an intersection of principal fractional ideals.  It cannot be principal:
if it were, its $D'$-endomorphism ring would be $D'$, whereas it contains
$U'$ because $\mathfrak n$ is a $U'$-ideal.

Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-divisorial-maximal} applied to $D'$ gives a proper
overring $D'+D'w$ and a relation $w^2=b+cw$ with $b,c\in D'$.
Choose $s\in D\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $sb,sc\in D$.
Then $(sw)^2=s^2b+(sc)(sw)$ has coefficients in $D$, and
$sw\notin D'$; in particular $sw\notin D$.  Thus in either case a
quadratic element outside $D$ has been found.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: descent of the coefficients to $R$.}\enspace Clear the two remaining coefficient denominators from $D=R_{\mathfrak p}$:
if $w_0^2=b_0+c_0w_0$ over $D$ and $w_0\notin D$, choose
$t\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ with $tb_0,tc_0\in R$, and put $z=tw_0$.
Then $z\notin D$ and $z^2=t^2b_0+(tc_0)z$ is a relation over $R$.
It yields $T=R+Rz$.  Its conductor is finitely generated by finite GF
duality.  If $c\in C\setminus\mathfrak p$, then $cz\in R$ would give
$z\in R_{\mathfrak p}$, a contradiction.  Thus $C\subseteq\mathfrak p$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-done
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-done}
For every commutative ring $R$, the class $\mathcal D_1(R)$ is closed under
extensions, kernels of epimorphisms between its members, direct summands,
and filtered colimits.  If $M\in\mathcal D_1(R)$ and $f\in R$, then
$M_f\in\mathcal D_1(R)$, with the dimension still taken over $R$.
Also, an ideal $I$ is Gorenstein flat if and only if
$R/I\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The extension, kernel, summand, and syzygy statements follow from
\cite[Theorems~2.8 and~2.11]{BennisGF} and the general closure theorem
\cite{SS}.  For filtered colimits, use the functorial
presentation by the free module on the underlying set of $M$.
Its kernel $\Omega(M)$ is Gorenstein flat precisely when
$M\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.
The underlying-set functor and the free-module functor commute with
filtered colimits. Exactness of filtered colimits then gives
$\Omega(\varinjlim M_\lambda)\cong\varinjlim\Omega(M_\lambda)$.  Apply the direct-limit
closure of Gorenstein flat modules.  Finally $M_f$ is the sequential
colimit of copies of $M$ under multiplication by $f$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-quadratic-if
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-quadratic-if}
Let $R$ be a domain satisfying $\mathrm{(O)}$, and let
$R\subsetneq T=R+Rx\subseteq\operatorname{Frac} R$ be an overring.  Put $C=(R:T)$ and
$A=R/C$.  Then $T$ and $C$ are totally reflexive $R$-modules, and $A$ is an
IF-ring.  In particular $A$ is coherent and self-FP-injective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: the dual modules.}\enspace We have $C=T^*$, and the finite duality in
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-finite-dual} gives $C\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.
The exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow C\xrightarrow{c\mapsto(-xc,c)}R^2
 \xrightarrow{(a,b)\mapsto a+bx}T\longrightarrow0
\]
therefore puts $T$ in $\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.  It and its dual $C$ are
totally reflexive.  Also $T/R\cong A$ by $r+C\mapsto rx+R$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: intermediate rings and annihilators.}\enspace Let $J$ be a finitely generated ideal of $A$ and $I$ its inverse image in
$R$.  The module $S=R+Ix$ is a ring: write $x^2=u+vx$ with $u,v\in R$ and
multiply its elements.  Since $C$ and $J$ are finitely generated, $S$ is
module-finite, hence Gorenstein flat by $\mathrm{(O)}$.  Put $D=(R:S)$.  Duality
gives that $D$ is finitely generated and $S=(R:D)$.  Direct calculation
shows
\[
 D/C=\operatorname{ann}_A J,\qquad
 J=\operatorname{ann}_A\operatorname{ann}_A J.
\]
For the second equality, for $r\in R$ one has
$rD\subseteq C$ if and only if $rx\in(R:D)=S$, if and only if $r\in I$.
Thus annihilators of finitely generated ideals of $A$ are finitely
generated and satisfy the double-annihilator identity.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: coherence and self-FP-injectivity.}\enspace These statements imply coherence: for finitely generated $J,L$,
\[
 J\cap L=\operatorname{ann}_A
       (\operatorname{ann}_A J+\operatorname{ann}_A L)
\]
is finitely generated, and annihilators of single elements are finitely
generated.  They also give self-FP-injectivity.  To extend a map from
$J+bA$ to $A$, first extend its restriction to $J$ by induction on the
number of generators and subtract that multiplication map.  Its value
$h$ at $b$ is then annihilated by $(J:b)$.  Since
$b\operatorname{ann}_A J$ is finitely generated,
\[
 \operatorname{ann}_A(J:b)
 =\operatorname{ann}_A\operatorname{ann}_A
       (b\operatorname{ann}_A J)
 =b\operatorname{ann}_A J.
\]
Choose $d\in\operatorname{ann}_A J$ with $bd=h$; multiplication by $d$
extends the remaining map.  The base case is the double-annihilator
identity for a principal ideal.  Hence every map from a finitely
generated ideal to $A$ extends to $A$.  To pass from ideals to a finitely generated submodule $L\subseteq A^n$,
project onto the last coordinate. Its image $J$ is finitely generated,
and its kernel is finitely generated by coherence. Extend a given map
on this kernel to $A^{n-1}$ by induction, subtract that extension, and
factor the remaining map through $J$. The ideal case then extends it
to the last copy of $A$. Hence maps from all finitely generated
submodules of finite free modules extend. Thus $A$ is self-FP-injective.  The equivalence with the IF property is
\cite[Theorem~2.6]{MTY}.
head: environment

label: lem:quotient-degree-one
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Finite duality and the two-generator presentation give that $T,C$
are totally reflexive over $R$, and
$A\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.  The sequence $0\to C\to R\to A\to0$
gives
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_R(A,R)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ext}_R^1(A,R)\cong T/R\cong A,\qquad
 \operatorname{Ext}_R^i(A,R)=0\quad(i>1).
\]
Choose the last identification so that the class of
\[
 \eta:\quad0\longrightarrow R\longrightarrow T
 \longrightarrow A\longrightarrow0
\]
corresponds to $1$.  This is possible because the connecting map
$R\to\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(A,R)$ for $\eta$ is surjective with kernel $C$.
Indeed, $T^*=C$ and $\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(T,R)=0$.

The vanishing of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(L,R)$ follows because $C\ne0$ annihilates
$L$ and $R$ is torsion-free. Take an injective resolution $E^\bullet$
of $R$. The complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,E^\bullet)$ consists of injective
$A$-modules and has its only cohomology in degree one, equal to $A$.
Its degree-zero monomorphism splits, because its source is injective.
Delete the resulting contractible summand and shift: the remaining
complex is an injective resolution of $A$.  Applying $\operatorname{Hom}_A(L,-)$
proves \eqref{eq:qcs-ext-shift}.  In degree one the identification sends
$\phi:L\to A$ to the pullback $\phi^*\eta$.
head: environment

label: lem:qcs-syzygy-lift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qcs-syzygy-lift}
Let $R$ be a domain and let $R\subsetneq T=R+Rx\subseteq\operatorname{Frac} R$
be an overring that is Gorenstein flat over $R$. Set $C=(R:T)$ and
$A=R/C$, and suppose that $A$ is an IF-ring.  If $N$ is a finitely presented $A$-module and
\[
 0\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow F\xrightarrow{\pi}N
 \longrightarrow0
\]
is a presentation with $F$ finitely generated free over $R$, then $H$ is
totally reflexive over $R$.
head: environment

label: eq:qcs-first-dual
title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: finite resolutions and the dual presentation.}\enspace
Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-degree-one} applies, and its proof shows
$A\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.
Since $A$ is coherent and self-FP-injective, every finitely presented
$A$-module is totally reflexive; use \cite[Theorem~2.6]{MTY} and finite
free resolutions over the coherent ring.  Put $N^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_A(N,A)$.
Thus $N,N^\vee\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(A)$,
$N\cong N^{\vee\vee}$, and their positive Ext groups into $A$ vanish.
They also belong to $\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.  To justify this last
assertion, all finite free $A$-modules belong to
$\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$; induction on $n$ along an $A$-resolution
by finitely generated free modules shows that every $\mathrm{FP}_\infty(A)$-module is
$\mathrm{FP}_n(R)$, for every $n$.

It follows that $H\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$ and
$\operatorname{Ext}_R^{>0}(H,R)=0$.  Dualizing the presentation of $N$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcs-first-dual}
 0\longrightarrow F^*\longrightarrow H^*\longrightarrow N^\vee
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
In particular $H^*\in\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$.  Dualizing again and using
\eqref{eq:qcs-ext-shift} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcs-second-dual}
 0\longrightarrow H^{**}\longrightarrow F
 \xrightarrow{\beta}N^{\vee\vee}
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(H^*,R)\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: identification of the biduality map.}\enspace We verify that $\beta$ is the composite of $\pi$ and evaluation
$N\to N^{\vee\vee}$, after making compatible choices of signs for the connecting maps.

For $\phi\in N^\vee$, lift $\phi\pi:F\to A$ through $T\to A$.
The restriction of a lift $\widetilde\phi:F\to T$ to $H$ lands in $R$
and represents $\phi$ in the quotient in
\eqref{eq:qcs-first-dual}.  Conversely, for each $h\in H^*$ choose
$\phi$ corresponding to its class.  Adjusting such a lift by a map
$F\to R$ makes its restriction equal to $h$.  This extension of $h$ to
$F\to T$ is unique, since $\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,T)=0$: $N$ is killed by the nonzero
ideal $C$, whereas $T$ is torsion-free.  For $u\in F$, evaluation of
these extensions at $u$ gives a map $H^*\to T$ extending
$F^*\to R$, $q\mapsto q(u)$.  Pushing out
\eqref{eq:qcs-first-dual} by this latter map identifies its extension
class with the pullback of $\eta$ along
\[
 N^\vee\longrightarrow A,\qquad
 \phi\longmapsto\phi(\pi(u)).
\]
This is precisely the connecting map defining $\beta(u)$.  Hence
$\beta(u)(\phi)=\phi(\pi(u))$, as claimed.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: the complete resolution.}\enspace Since evaluation $N\to N^{\vee\vee}$ is an isomorphism,
\eqref{eq:qcs-second-dual} identifies $H^{**}$ with $H$ through its
natural map and gives $\operatorname{Ext}_R^1(H^*,R)=0$.  For $i>1$,
\eqref{eq:qcs-first-dual} and \eqref{eq:qcs-ext-shift} give
$\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(H^*,R)=0$.  Thus $H$ and $H^*$ are
$\mathrm{FP}_\infty$, $H\cong H^{**}$, and their positive Ext groups
into $R$ vanish.  Splice a resolution by finitely generated free modules of $H$ with the
dual of one of $H^*$ to obtain the required totally acyclic complex.
Applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,E)$ to its exact dual for an injective $E$
shows that the complex is a complete flat resolution as well.
head: environment

label: thm:qcs-return
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:qcs-return}
Let $R$ be a domain, and let $R\subsetneq T=R+Rx\subseteq\operatorname{Frac} R$
be an overring that is Gorenstein flat as an $R$-module,
put $C=(R:T)$, and suppose that $R/C$ is an IF-ring.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{Gfd}_R N\le1\qquad\text{for every }R/C\text{-module }N.
\]
More generally the same bound holds for every $R$-module $N$ such that
each element of $N$ is annihilated by some power of $C$.
Consequently, if $R$ satisfies $\mathrm{(O)}$, these assertions apply to every
proper two-generated module overring.  For every ideal $J$ of $R$ they give
\[
 C\subseteq\sqrt J\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\in\mathcal{GF}(R).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The finitely presented $R/C$-modules have the asserted bound by
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-syzygy-lift}.  Every $R/C$-module is a filtered colimit
of finitely presented modules, so Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-done} gives the bound
for all of them, over $R$.

If $C^nN=0$, the finite filtration by $C^jN$ has factors annihilated by
$C$; extension closure gives $N\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.  In the elementwise
case take the increasing union of $\{y\in N:C^ny=0\}$ and use filtered
colimits.  Under $\mathrm{(O)}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-quadratic-if} supplies the IF
hypothesis.  Finally $C$ is finitely generated, so $C\subseteq\sqrt J$
implies $C^n\subseteq J$ for some $n$.  Apply the bound to $R/J$ and then
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-done}.
head: environment

label: lem:cp-product-torsion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cp-product-torsion}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $C_1,\ldots,C_s$ be ideals such that
every $R/C_j$-module belongs to $\mathcal D_1(R)$.  Put
$P=C_1\cdots C_s$.  Then every $R$-module whose elements are annihilated
by powers of $P$ belongs to $\mathcal D_1(R)$.
For $s=0$, use $P=R$; the assertion then concerns only the zero module.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $P^nN=0$ for a fixed $n$.  Starting with $N$, multiply
successively by $C_1,\ldots,C_s$, and repeat this list $n$ times.  This
gives a finite filtration ending in $P^nN=0$.  Each factor is annihilated
by one $C_j$, so extension closure puts $N$ in $\mathcal D_1(R)$.
For elementwise annihilation, write
$N=\bigcup_{n\ge1}(0:_N P^n)$ and use filtered-colimit closure from
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-done}.  The empty-product convention is immediate.
head: environment

label: lem:cp-bounded-complex
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cp-bounded-complex}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let
$X^0\to X^1\to\cdots\to X^r$ be a cochain complex with zero terms outside
$0,\ldots,r$.  Suppose that $X^i\in\mathcal D_1(R)$ for $i>0$, and that
$H^i(X^\bullet)\in\mathcal D_1(R)$ for every $i\ge0$.  Then
$X^0\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $r=0$ is immediate.  Write
$Z^i=\ker d^i$ and $B^i=\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$.
At the top, $Z^r=X^r$ and
$B^r=\ker(X^r\to H^r(X^\bullet))$ belong to $\mathcal D_1(R)$.
Descending induction uses
\[
 0\longrightarrow Z^i\longrightarrow X^i\longrightarrow B^{i+1}
 \longrightarrow0,\qquad
 0\longrightarrow B^i\longrightarrow Z^i\longrightarrow H^i(X^\bullet)
 \longrightarrow0
\]
for $i=r-1,\ldots,1$.  Kernel closure gives $B^1\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.
Finally $0\to H^0(X^\bullet)\to X^0\to B^1\to0$ and extension closure
prove the result.  All these closure properties are those of
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-done}.
head: environment

label: prop:cp-finite-patching
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:cp-power-containment
title: Proof
body_md:
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: the finite annihilator bound.}\enspace Put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $P=C_1\cdots C_s$, with $P=R$ if $s=0$.
The covering gives
\[
 V(I+J)\subseteq V(P),\qquad P\subseteq\sqrt{I+J}.
\]
The ideal $P$ is finitely generated, so some $e\ge1$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cp-power-containment}
 P^e\subseteq I+J.
\end{equation}
Every module annihilated by $I$ and elementwise annihilated by powers
of $J$ is therefore elementwise annihilated by powers of $P$.
It belongs to $\mathcal D_1(R)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cp-product-torsion}.

\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: the localization complex and its cohomology.}\enspace If $r=0$, \eqref{eq:cp-power-containment} gives $P^eB=0$, proving the
result.  Suppose $r\ge1$.  Form the finite augmented localization complex
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cp-cech}
 X^\bullet
 = B\otimes_R\bigotimes_{i=1}^r[\,R\longrightarrow R_{f_i}\,],
\end{equation}
where each two-term factor has degrees zero and one, with the usual
signs on the tensor product differential.  Thus
\[
 X^0=B,\qquad
 X^q=\bigoplus_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_q\le r}
        B_{f_{i_1}\cdots f_{i_q}}\quad(1\le q\le r).
\]
For $q>0$, every summand is a localization of one of the modules
$B_{f_i}$ in the hypothesis, so $X^q\in\mathcal D_1(R)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-done}.

After localizing \eqref{eq:cp-cech} at $f_i$, its $i$th two-term factor
is the identity complex $[R_{f_i}\xrightarrow{1}R_{f_i}]$.
Consequently $X^\bullet_{f_i}$ is contractible, and
$H^q(X^\bullet)_{f_i}=0$ for every $i,q$.  For any cohomology element
$h$, choose $n_i\ge1$ with $f_i^{n_i}h=0$.
Then $J^Nh=0$ for $N=1+\sum_i(n_i-1)$, by expansion of products of the
generators of $J$.  Also $Ih=0$, since the complex consists of
$B$-modules.  Equation~\eqref{eq:cp-power-containment} gives
$P^{eN}h=0$.  Hence all $H^q(X^\bullet)$ belong to $\mathcal D_1(R)$.
\par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: descending through the bounded complex.}\enspace
Lemma~\ref{lem:cp-bounded-complex} gives $X^0=B\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.
This uses only extensions and kernels of epimorphisms between modules
in $\mathcal D_1(R)$, not unrestricted closure under cokernels.
The argument does not identify the displayed cohomology with derived
local cohomology and imposes no weak-proregularity condition.
head: environment

label: lem:cp-cover-selection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cp-cover-selection}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $I$ an ideal.  Suppose that every
$\mathfrak p\in V(I)$ belongs to a member of a family of subsets of
$\operatorname{Spec} R$, each of the form $D(f)$ or $V(C)$ with $C$ finitely generated.
Then finitely many members of this family cover $V(I)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each indicated set is open in the constructible topology.
The subset $V(I)=\bigcap_{a\in I}V(a)$ is closed in that compact
Hausdorff space.  Apply compactness of $V(I)$.
head: environment

label: prop:cp-finite-certificate
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\mathfrak p\supseteq I$.  If $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is integrally closed,
then it is a valuation domain by Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-normal}, since
$\mathrm{(O)}$ localizes.  Some nonzero generator $a\in I$ generates
$I_{\mathfrak p}$.  Clearing the coefficient denominators of the finitely
many generators of $I$ yields $f\notin\mathfrak p$ with $I_f=aR_f$.
This supplies a set $D(f)$ containing $\mathfrak p$.

If $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is not integrally closed,
Theorem~\ref{thm:qcs-quadratic-witness} supplies a proper quadratic module
overring $T=R+Rz$ with a nonzero finitely generated conductor
$C\subseteq\mathfrak p$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-quadratic-if} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:qcs-return} give the asserted bound for all $R/C$-modules.
This supplies the set $V(C)$ containing $\mathfrak p$.

Doing this for every prime over $I$ gives a constructibly open covering.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cp-cover-selection} extracts a finite subcover.
The final containment follows as in
\eqref{eq:cp-power-containment}.
head: environment

label: thm:cp-main
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $R$ is $G$-Pr\"ufer, every torsion-free $R$-module is Gorenstein flat
by \cite[Corollary~2.4]{HLZ}; this includes every overring.  Thus
(i) implies (ii), and (ii) implies (iii).  Every overring is the directed
union of its finitely generated $R$-subalgebras, so the direct-limit
closure in \cite{SS} proves (iii) implies
(ii).

Assume (ii).  It suffices to prove that every finitely generated ideal
of $R$ is Gorenstein flat.  The zero and unit ideals are immediate.
For a nonzero finitely generated proper ideal $I$, use the data in
Proposition~\ref{prop:cp-finite-certificate}.  Each $I_{f_i}=a_iR_{f_i}$
gives an exact sequence of $R$-modules
\[
 0\longrightarrow R_{f_i}\xrightarrow{a_i}R_{f_i}
 \longrightarrow(R/I)_{f_i}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Both copies of $R_{f_i}$ are flat over $R$, and the first map is injective
because $R$ is a domain and $a_i\ne0$.  Hence
$(R/I)_{f_i}\in\mathcal D_1(R)$.  The other hypotheses of
Proposition~\ref{prop:cp-finite-patching} are supplied by the same
finite certificate.  That proposition yields
$\operatorname{Gfd}_R(R/I)\le1$.  The syzygy criterion therefore makes $I$ Gorenstein
flat.

The ideal characterization in Section~\ref{sec:qcs-preliminaries}
now gives the $G$-Pr\"ufer property, including coherence and
$\operatorname{fd}_R E\le1$ for every injective $E$. This proves (ii) implies (i).
head: environment

label: cor:cp-normal-conclusion
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:cp-normal-conclusion}
An integrally closed domain whose overrings are Gorenstein flat is a
classical Pr\"ufer domain.  For an arbitrary domain satisfying the overring
condition, every finitely generated ideal has a complete resolution by
finitely generated projective modules, and every torsion-free module is
Gorenstein flat.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The normal assertion is Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-normal}.
In general Theorem~\ref{thm:cp-main} gives coherence and Gorenstein
flatness of every finitely generated ideal.  Such ideals belong to
$\mathrm{FP}_\infty(R)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:qcs-finite-dual} gives their
complete resolutions by finitely generated free modules.  The torsion-free assertion is
\cite[Corollary~2.4]{HLZ}.
head: environment

label: ex:overring-cusp
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:overring-cusp}
Let $k$ be a field, $R=k[[t^2,t^3]]$, and $V=k[[t]]$.
Then every overring of $R$ is Gorenstein flat over $R$, but $R$ is not
Pr\"ufer and the module-finite normalization $V=R+Rt$ is not flat over $R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The presentation $R\cong k[[u,v]]/(v^2-u^3)$ makes $R$ a
one-dimensional Noetherian Gorenstein local domain. Its torsion-free
modules are Gorenstein flat by the standard Gorenstein and domain
characterizations \cite{CFH,HLZ}. The element $t=t^3/t^2$ is integral
over $R$ but does not belong to $R$, so $R$ is not integrally closed
and hence is not Pr\"ufer. If $V$ were flat, its finite presentation
over the Noetherian local ring $R$ would make it free. Its rank is one,
whereas $V/(t^2,t^3)V=V/t^2V$ has $k$-dimension two. This is impossible.
head: environment

label: ex:modulefinite-insufficient
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:modulefinite-insufficient}
Let $k$ be a field and let $R=k[u,v]_{(u,v)}$.
Its only module-finite overring is $R$, but the finite-type overring
$T=R[v/u]$ satisfies $\operatorname{fd}_RT=\operatorname{Gfd}_RT=1$.
In particular, testing only module-finite overrings does not
characterize Gorenstein Pr\"ufer domains.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ring $R$ is an integrally closed domain, so a module-finite overring,
being integral, must equal $R$. Gauss's lemma in the UFD $R$ gives
$T\cong R[Z]/(uZ-v)$ and an exact sequence of free $R$-modules
\[
 0\longrightarrow R[Z]\xrightarrow{\,uZ-v\,}R[Z]
 \longrightarrow T\longrightarrow0.
\]
Tensoring with the residue field $k$ makes the displayed differential
zero, so $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(k,T)\cong k[Z]\ne0$ and $\operatorname{fd}_RT=1$.
A module of finite flat dimension has the same Gorenstein flat dimension
\cite[Theorem~2.2]{Bennis}. Thus $T$ is not Gorenstein flat over $R$.
It cannot be module-finite, since it is a proper overring of $R$.
head: environment
